overview: The file combines a 1932 exchange between Harold K. Hochschild of the American Metal Company and State Department Far Eastern Affairs chief Stanley K. Hornbeck concerning Japan’s supplies of the munitions-related nonferrous metals lead, zinc, and copper, with a later American consular report on the rapid expansion of aluminum and hydroelectric-power production in Japanese-ruled Taiwan. The correspondence records trade impressions that Japan continued conspicuous foreign purchases of lead and zinc during the global industrial depression while possessing substantial copper capacity. The 1938 report supplies detailed figures, costs, locations, and construction schedules for aluminum works and four associated power plants in eastern Taiwan; it was recopied and filed for wartime use in 1944.

subfiles.title: Hochschild letter on Japan’s requirements for lead, zinc, and copper
subfiles.about: Hochschild conveys metal-trade assessments of Japan’s production and foreign purchasing of three nonferrous metals important to munitions.
subfiles.summary: Hochschild reports that Japan has practically no domestic lead production and regularly purchases large quantities in non-American markets, where prices are lower than in the tariff-protected United States. Although recent statistics are incomplete, the trade believes Japanese lead and zinc buying has remained unusually active while other countries’ purchases have declined during the industrial depression. Japan has some zinc output but supplements it with imports, whereas its potential copper production is believed substantially to exceed domestic industrial requirements; Hochschild offers to provide figures if desired.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of Hochschild’s metal-market comments
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges and expresses appreciation for Hochschild’s comments on Japanese lead, copper, and zinc requirements.
subfiles.summary: The reply thanks Hochschild for his letter of February 25 and for supplying comments about Japan’s requirements for lead, copper, and zinc. It also recalls their meeting at the Wednesday-night dinner. The contextual attribution is to Stanley K. Hornbeck, although the OCR has plainly garbled the signature line.

subfiles.title: Gerald Warner report on aluminum production in Taiwan
subfiles.to: Commercial Office, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: The report describes current and projected aluminum-smelting capacity in Taiwan and the hydroelectric developments intended to supply a new eastern Taiwan factory.
subfiles.summary: The Japan Aluminum Company’s Takao plant, producing 6,000 metric tons annually since October 1937, was expected soon to reach 8,000 tons and possibly 9,000. A new factory at Beiron in Karenko City was projected to produce 8,000 tons annually by 1941, supported by the Kiyomizu No. 1 and No. 2, Hatsune, and Domon hydroelectric plants. Together the plants were to provide 36,970 kilowatts at a total construction cost of ¥11,058,000, with completion stages extending through 1940 and machinery and materials supplied from or through Japan Proper. Based on the Taiwan Nichi Nichi Newspaper, the report was completed November 1 and mailed November 2, 1938; copies were made for Far Eastern Affairs liaison on August 4, 1944, and filed August 17, 1944.

interest: The file is valuable for juxtaposing private American commodity intelligence with official consular reporting on Japan’s strategic-metals position. Hochschild’s cautious distinction between incomplete statistics and the impressions of the metal trade illuminates how officials assessed Japanese rearmament-related demand during the Depression. Warner’s report is unusually useful for its plant-by-plant capacities, costs, and completion schedules, while its 1944 copying and filing show how prewar economic reporting was repurposed for wartime intelligence on Japanese-controlled industrial infrastructure.
